ab_carrot_cave.blurb: A steep cave feature up the canyon of Carrot Creek in the Bow Valley near Canmore, and the last sport sector as you head upstream, a short walk beyond the first wall. Its twelve sport routes are all hard: four in the 5.12 range, seven at 5.13 and a single 5.14, so this is a spot for strong redpointers rather than people building mileage. The limestone is overhanging and development mostly dates from the 1990s, so give the older fixed hardware a careful look before trusting it. The cave keeps its shade well into late afternoon in winter, takes water running over it in spring, and turns very hot in summer.
ab_carrot_cave.approach: Follow the canyon upstream until the cave comes into view up on your left, roughly 200 m past where the canyon pinches in.

ab_sofa_king_area.blurb: A big boulder with a few smaller ones around it, sitting close to the road at the north-west end of the Frank Slide boulder field in the Crowsnest Pass. It is among the first blocks reached on the trail, so it makes a handy warm-up stop before heading on to the larger House Area boulders. There are twelve problems on limestone, mostly easy to moderate: three at V0, four at V1, two at V2, one V3 and two at V5. Good for a short session or for climbers who want a range of lower grades near the car.

ab_the_cave.blurb: A large cave low in the cliff band of The Lookout, in Echo Canyon above Canmore. It is the first stretch of rock you meet on the trail up past the Hideaway. Twelve sport routes, split evenly between the 5.12 and 5.13 ranges, make it a destination for experienced climbers, with holds that run from mid-sized to big. Many lines are often damp, so pick a dry spell. The main wall nearby sees sun from mid-morning to early afternoon, and the wider Lookout area is best in the shoulder seasons when the rock is warm but the sun is weaker.

ab_amphitheater.blurb: A recessed section of the quartzite cliff band at the back of Lake Louise in Banff National Park. Unlike most of the neighbouring walls, the rock here is not steep or overhanging, which makes it a friendly place for moderate climbing. Of its twelve routes, eight are trad, including a few two-pitch lines, and four are sport. Grades lean moderate: one easy route, four in the 5.8 to 5.9 band, six at 5.10 and a single 5.11. A good choice for climbers stepping up from the easy end of the grade scale.
ab_amphitheater.approach: Walk the trail along the lake until it ends; the crag sits in a recessed notch of the cliff band, above a slope of scree.

ab_the_rectory.blurb: The wall at Grassi Lakes, above Canmore in the Bow Valley, where the area's hardest sport routes cluster. Twelve limestone lines are on offer: one in the 5.11 range, nine at 5.12 and two at 5.13, so it suits climbers comfortable on difficult grades. Expect edges, cracks and a bit of everything between. A group of boulders at the foot of the wall helps you recognise it. Grassi Lakes in general is a good escape when the valley bottom is baking in summer.
ab_the_rectory.approach: Walk down from the dam into the climbing area, pass The Ghetto and its long stairway, and continue until the ground levels out; a cluster of boulders marks the base of the wall.

ab_sumc_buttress.blurb: A small sport crag tucked into the forest at the left end of a cliff band in Heart Creek, east of Canmore in the Bow Valley. It holds twelve limestone sport routes, almost all of them in the middle of the grade range: nine at 5.10, with a couple of 5.9s and one 5.8. That makes it a comfortable place for climbers who lead 5.10 and want a mellow day. Heart Creek as a whole is a summer venue, with routes of about 30 m, short walks from the trail and plenty of weekend traffic.

ab_punter_palace.blurb: A steep, dark-streaked patch of closely bolted rock on the west side of the north face of Tunnel Mountain, right beside the town of Banff. All twelve routes are sport and they are hard for the most part: one at 5.10, two at 5.11, three at 5.12, five at 5.13 and a lone 5.14. Several lines cross or merge, and most finish on a slab that is longer than the overhanging part below. The belay ledge is cramped and fits only one or two parties. Reaching it means weaving through mountain-bike trails, then scrambling the left side of a ramp.
ab_punter_palace.approach: Spot the rock panel from the road, follow a mix of maintained bike trails and faint climbers' paths toward the bottom of the ramp, then scramble up its left side to the belay area. Take care not to knock rocks onto the people below.

ab_multipitch_ground_level.blurb: A north-east-facing limestone cliff by Emerald Lake near Crowsnest Pass, with twelve climbs reached from the bottom up: ten sport routes, one trad line and one aid route. Grades run from easy 5.7 up to 5.11, with the bulk in the 5.8 to 5.10 band, so mid-grade parties are well served. The wall faces away from the afternoon sun, which makes it a good pick for hot summer days, and the short walk from the car park keeps the day simple. The lake itself is chilly but makes a welcome dip after climbing.
ab_multipitch_ground_level.parking_note: Take Highway 3 toward Crowsnest Lake and turn south, then branch right onto the gravel road. After roughly half a kilometre it becomes pavement, which continues for about a kilometre and a half to a car park at its end.
ab_multipitch_ground_level.approach: The cliff is a short walk of about three minutes from the car park.
